questions.question: What is the synchronized keyword in Java and what does it prevent?
questions.title: synchronized Keyword in Java
questions.direct_answer: The synchronized keyword ensures that only one thread at a time can execute a synchronized method or block. It prevents race conditions by acquiring an intrinsic lock (monitor) on an object before executing the code, guaranteeing both atomicity and visibility of shared data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core multithreading knowledge—synchronized is the most fundamental synchronization mechanism in Java.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what object the lock is acquired on, or thinking synchronized only prevents simultaneous execution without understanding the memory visibility guarantee.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the intrinsic lock concept and the difference between synchronized method versus synchronized block, including which object holds the lock in each case.

sections.title: Understanding synchronized and Thread Safety
sections.content:
The **`synchronized`** keyword lets only one thread run a piece of code at a time. You put it on a method or a block, and Java turns that region into a **critical section**.

Think of a single-occupancy room. The first person in locks the door, everyone else waits, and the next person enters only when it's free.

Under the hood, `synchronized` uses an **intrinsic lock** (also called a **monitor**) that every Java object carries. When a thread enters a synchronized region, it acquires the lock on that object. Other threads that want a synchronized region on the **same** object wait until the lock is free. This buys you two things: **atomicity** (the steps finish without interruption) and **visibility** (one thread's changes become visible to the others). Without it, threads can read stale cached values or interleave steps and corrupt shared data.

sections.title: One Thread at a Time on the Monitor
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant L as Monitor lock
    participant B as Thread B
    A->>L: acquire lock
    Note over A: runs critical section
    B->>L: tries to acquire
    Note over B: BLOCKED, waits
    A->>L: release lock
    L-->>B: lock granted
    Note over B: now runs safely
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|synchronized|~One thread at a time|acquires monitor lock|mutual exclusion|releases on exit
blue|Two Forms|~Method or block|method locks this/Class|block locks chosen object|narrower is better
emerald|Guarantees|~More than mutex|atomicity of section|visibility (happens-before)|memory flush
violet|Cost|~Contention|threads go BLOCKED|keep section small|don't over-synchronize

sections.title: Wrong: an unsynchronized withdraw can overspend
Right: synchronized makes withdraw atomic
When to Use synchronized
sections.content:
Use synchronized when multiple threads need to modify shared mutable state like counters, collections, or complex objects. In a Spring REST API, if you have an in-memory cache that multiple request threads access, synchronize the update methods to prevent corruption.

Use it for business logic that must execute atomically—like transferring money between accounts where you debit one and credit another as a single logical operation. For simple read-heavy scenarios with occasional writes, consider **ReentrantReadWriteLock** instead. For single-variable updates like incrementing a counter, prefer **AtomicInteger** which is faster. Synchronized is your go-to for protecting any multi-step operation on shared data where consistency matters.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing on the wrong object**: Freshers often synchronize on different objects thinking they're protecting the same data—if Thread A locks on `lockA` and Thread B locks on `lockB`, both enter the critical section simultaneously. The lock object must be shared.
- **Synchronizing local variables**: Writing `synchronized(localVar)` in a method where each thread gets its own `localVar` instance provides zero protection—you need a shared lock object.
- **Forgetting static synchronized locks the Class object**: A static synchronized method doesn't lock instance methods, so instance and static synchronized methods can run concurrently, potentially causing issues if they touch shared static fields.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Intrinsic lock**: Every Java object has a built-in monitor lock that synchronized uses—you don't create locks explicitly, they're always there
- **Instance method**: synchronized instance method locks on `this`, so two threads calling different synchronized methods on the same object will block each other
- **Static method**: synchronized static method locks on the Class object (e.g., `BankAccount.class`), separate from instance locks
- **Memory visibility**: synchronized creates a happens-before relationship—all writes before releasing the lock are visible to threads that subsequently acquire the same lock
- **Reentrant**: A thread holding a lock can re-enter any synchronized block using the same lock without deadlocking itself
- **Performance cost**: Acquiring and releasing locks involves OS-level operations, so overusing synchronized on hot paths can slow your application
- **No lock object for primitives**: You can't synchronize on int, boolean, etc.—only reference types have monitors

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The synchronized keyword makes sure only one thread executes a piece of code at a time. It's how you prevent race conditions in Java. When you mark a method as synchronized, the JVM locks the object that method belongs to. So if I have a synchronized withdraw method on a BankAccount object, and Thread A is executing it, Thread B trying to call the same method on that same account has to wait. The lock is on the object itself—every Java object has what's called an intrinsic lock or monitor. You can also use synchronized blocks where you explicitly say which object to lock on. That gives you finer control—you might lock just the part of the method that touches shared data, not the whole method. There's also a memory visibility guarantee. Without synchronized, one thread might cache a variable value and not see updates another thread made. Synchronized forces cache flushes so threads see the latest values. One thing freshers miss is knowing what object the lock is on. For instance methods it's the this object. For static methods it's the Class object like BankAccount dot class. If you synchronize on the wrong object, you get no protection at all. That's the key—synchronized is both about mutual exclusion and memory consistency.

questions.question: What is a race condition and how does synchronized prevent it?
questions.title: Race Condition and synchronized Prevention
questions.direct_answer: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access and modify shared data concurrently, and the final result depends on the unpredictable timing of thread execution. The synchronized keyword prevents race conditions by ensuring only one thread at a time can execute the critical section that modifies the shared state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can explain race conditions with a concrete example, not just abstract theory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying two threads run at the same time without explaining why concurrent access to shared data produces incorrect results.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the read-modify-write sequence at the CPU instruction level using the classic counter increment example, showing how operations interleave.

sections.title: What Race Conditions Are and Why They Matter
sections.content:
A **race condition** happens when multiple threads compete to access and modify shared data, and the program's correctness depends on the unpredictable order and timing of thread execution. It's called a race because the threads are racing to the data—whoever gets there first and at what exact microsecond determines the outcome. Imagine two bank tellers processing withdrawals from the same account simultaneously, both reading the balance before either writes the updated value back.

The result depends on whose write happens last, potentially allowing overdrafts. At the CPU level, operations like `count++` that look atomic in Java source code actually break down into three machine instructions: **read** the current value from memory, **increment** it in a register, **write** the result back. If two threads interleave these steps, you get lost updates. Without synchronization, the JVM and CPU are free to reorder and cache operations for performance, making the problem worse. The **synchronized** keyword solves this by creating a **critical section**—a region of code where only one thread can execute at a time, eliminating the race.

sections.title: How an Interleaving Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread A reads count] --> B[Adds one in register] B --> C[Writes count back] A2[Thread B reads
the same old value] --> C2[Writes the same number] C --> D{Both wrote
the same value?} C2 --> D D -- Yes --> E[One update is lost] ```

sections.content:
amber|Race Condition|~Timing-dependent bug|interleaved read-modify-write|count++ not atomic|lost updates
blue|synchronized Fix|~Serialize access|one thread in section|atomic and visible|consistent result
emerald|Shared State|~The root cause|mutable and shared|multiple writers|needs protection
violet|Alternatives|~Beyond synchronized|AtomicInteger|ConcurrentHashMap|immutability

sections.title: Wrong: count++ races across threads
Right: synchronized serializes the increment
Where Race Conditions Occur in Real Systems
sections.content:
Race conditions appear whenever threads share mutable state without coordination. In a Spring web application, if you have a shared cache updated by multiple request threads, race conditions can corrupt cache entries or cause lost updates. Session counters, rate limiters, and metrics aggregators are common hotspots—ten threads incrementing a request counter simultaneously will lose counts without synchronization. In e-commerce systems, inventory updates are classic race condition territory: two threads read inventory as 5 units, both decrement to 4, both write back 4, and you've sold two items but only decremented once.

Use synchronized, **ReentrantLock**, or atomic classes like **AtomicInteger** to guard these critical sections. Even seemingly thread-safe collections like **ConcurrentHashMap** don't prevent race conditions in compound operations like check-then-act patterns.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single Java statements are atomic**: Freshers think `count++` is a single indivisible operation, but it compiles to multiple bytecode instructions that can interleave. Only assignments of references and primitives up to 32 bits are atomic without synchronization.
- **Not synchronizing reads**: Protecting writes with synchronized but leaving reads unsynchronized still causes race conditions—readers might see partially updated state or stale cached values.
- **Using separate lock objects**: If Thread A synchronizes on `lockA` and Thread B synchronizes on `lockB` while accessing the same shared variable, both can enter the critical section simultaneously because they're not contending for the same lock.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Read-modify-write**: Operations like increment, decrement, or check-then-update involve reading a value, computing a new one, and writing it back—race conditions occur when these steps interleave across threads
- **Non-atomic operations**: In Java, only reading and writing reference variables and primitives (except long and double) are guaranteed atomic without synchronization
- **Lost updates**: The classic symptom—two threads increment a counter 1000 times each, but the final count is less than 2000 because writes overwrote each other
- **Check-then-act**: Patterns like if balance greater than amount then withdraw are inherently racy unless the entire sequence is synchronized on a shared lock
- **Visibility and ordering**: Race conditions aren't just about simultaneous access—CPU caching and instruction reordering can make changes invisible to other threads without synchronization
- **Critical section**: The synchronized block that protects shared data must cover the entire logical operation, not just individual field accesses
- **Happens-before**: synchronized establishes ordering guarantees—all writes before releasing a lock are visible to threads that subsequently acquire the same lock

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A race condition is when two or more threads access shared data at the same time, and the result depends on which thread wins the race. The outcome is unpredictable. The classic example is incrementing a counter. Let's say you have count equals ten. Thread A reads it, gets ten, increments to eleven. But before Thread A writes eleven back, Thread B also reads the original value—still ten—increments it to eleven, and writes eleven. Now both threads wrote eleven, so the counter is eleven instead of twelve. One update got lost. This happens because count plus plus isn't atomic. It's actually three CPU instructions: load the value from memory, add one in a register, store it back. When threads interleave those instructions, you get corruption. The synchronized keyword prevents this by making sure only one thread executes the critical section at a time. When Thread A enters the synchronized block, it locks the object. Thread B has to wait. Thread A reads, increments, writes, and unlocks. Then Thread B can go. No interleaving, no lost update. Another thing is memory visibility. Even if you avoid interleaving, without synchronization, Thread B might read a stale cached value of count. Synchronized forces cache flushes so threads see the latest writes. That's why you need synchronization on both reads and writes, not just writes.

questions.question: What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?
questions.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block
questions.direct_answer: A synchronized method locks the entire method on this (for instance methods) or the Class object (for static methods). A synchronized block locks only a specified section of code and lets you choose which object to lock on. Synchronized blocks offer better performance through finer-grained locking—you can protect only the critical section rather than the entire method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of synchronization granularity and the ability to choose appropriate locking strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing you can specify a different lock object in a synchronized block, or thinking synchronized methods and blocks are completely interchangeable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that synchronized blocks reduce the critical section size, improving concurrency by allowing multiple threads to execute non-conflicting parts of the method simultaneously.

sections.title: Synchronized Methods vs Blocks: Choosing Granularity
sections.content:
A **synchronized method** locks an entire method. A **synchronized block** locks only the lines you wrap. Both stop race conditions, but they differ in **granularity** and **flexibility**.

A synchronized method locks a fixed object: `this` for instance methods, or the `Class` object for static methods. You don't choose the lock. A synchronized block lets you lock just a portion of a method and pick the lock object yourself.

This matters for performance. Picture locking a whole room versus locking just one desk. If your method does I/O or logging that never touches shared state, locking the entire method makes threads wait for no reason. A synchronized block wraps only the few lines that change shared fields, so the lock is held for microseconds instead of milliseconds. You can also use different lock objects for independent data, which lets unrelated threads run in parallel.

sections.title: Method Lock vs Block Lock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB M[Synchronized method] --> M1[Locks whole method on this] M1 --> M2[Other threads wait
for the entire body] B[Synchronized block] --> B1[Locks only chosen lines] B1 --> B2[Rest of the method
runs in parallel] ```

sections.content:
amber|Synchronized Method|~Locks whole method|this for instance|Class for static|coarse-grained
blue|Synchronized Block|~Locks a region|choose the monitor|smaller critical section|finer control
emerald|Why Block Wins|~Less contention|lock only shared part|private lock object|avoid locking this
violet|Trap|~Locking on this|external code can lock too|use private final Object|prevents interference

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Block
sections.content:
| Aspect | Synchronized Method | Synchronized Block |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lock Object | Implicit: this or Class | Explicit: any object you specify |
| Scope | Entire method body | Only the code inside the block |
| Flexibility | Fixed—can't choose lock | Choose lock per data structure |
| Performance | Holds lock longer | Holds lock only for critical section |
| Readability | Cleaner for simple cases | More verbose but more control |

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use a **synchronized method** when the entire method body accesses shared state and needs protection—like a simple getter/setter or a short operation that's entirely critical. It's clean and readable for straightforward cases.

Use a **synchronized block** when you have a long method where only a small portion touches shared data. For example, if your method parses a request, does validation, then updates a shared cache, synchronize only the cache update line.

Use different lock objects in synchronized blocks when protecting independent data structures—like separate locks for a user map and an order map in a service class. This allows threads working on users and threads working on orders to run in parallel. In high-throughput systems, reducing the critical section size by even a few microseconds can double your concurrency. Synchronized blocks also let you implement advanced patterns like lock ordering to prevent deadlocks by always acquiring locks in a consistent sequence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing on a local variable**: Freshers write synchronized on a variable declared inside the method, so each thread gets its own lock instance and no coordination happens—the lock object must be shared across threads.
- **Mixing method and block locks on the same object**: If some methods use synchronized method (locking on this) and others use synchronized block on a different object, they don't coordinate, and you still have race conditions.
- **Locking on a collection you're iterating**: Synchronizing on a list object while iterating doesn't prevent concurrent modification if other code adds/removes elements without locking the same object—use explicit lock objects or concurrent collections.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Implicit vs explicit lock**: Synchronized methods lock on this or the Class object automatically; synchronized blocks require you to specify synchronized on which object
- **Critical section size**: The lock is held only while executing the synchronized code—smaller blocks mean less contention and higher concurrency
- **Lock object choice**: You can lock on any object, including private final fields created just to serve as locks, giving you fine-grained control
- **Reentrant behavior**: Both methods and blocks use Java's intrinsic locks, which are reentrant—a thread holding a lock can re-acquire it without deadlocking itself
- **Static vs instance**: Synchronized static methods lock on the Class object, synchronized instance methods lock on this—they don't block each other
- **Performance trade-off**: Synchronized methods are simpler to write but synchronized blocks with minimal critical sections scale better under load
- **Null lock object**: Attempting synchronized on a null reference throws NullPointerException at runtime—always ensure lock objects are initialized

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A synchronized method locks the entire method. For instance methods, it locks on the this object. For static methods, it locks on the Class object. You don't get to choose—it's automatic. A synchronized block, on the other hand, lets you lock just part of a method and you explicitly say which object to lock on. So you might have a long method that does some calculations and then updates a shared counter. With a synchronized method, you'd lock the whole thing. With a synchronized block, you lock only the two lines that touch the counter. That's way faster because other threads can execute the non-synchronized parts in parallel. You also get more flexibility with synchronized blocks. You can use different lock objects for different data structures. Say you have a user cache and an order cache in the same class. You create two separate lock objects and synchronize on the appropriate one. Now threads working on users don't block threads working on orders. They run concurrently. With synchronized methods, everything locks on this, so there's no parallelism. One thing freshers mess up is synchronizing on a local variable they created inside the method. That gives you zero protection because each thread has its own copy of that local variable. The lock object has to be shared—usually a field of the class. For simple cases, synchronized methods are cleaner. For performance-critical code with large methods, use synchronized blocks to minimize the time you hold the lock.

questions.question: What is AtomicInteger and when would you use it instead of synchronized?
questions.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized in Java
questions.direct_answer: AtomicInteger is a class from the java.util.concurrent.atomic package that provides thread-safe integer operations using non-blocking CPU-level compare-and-swap (CAS) instructions instead of locks. It's faster than synchronized for single-variable operations because CAS is a hardware instruction that doesn't block threads or require OS-level context switching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern concurrency utilities beyond the basic synchronized keyword—java.util.concurrent is essential for production Java.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing AtomicInteger exists, or thinking it's just a wrapper around synchronized when it actually uses fundamentally different lock-free algorithms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the non-blocking nature of CAS (compare-and-swap) and why it scales better under high contention—failed CAS operations retry immediately without blocking the thread.

sections.title: AtomicInteger: Lock-Free Thread Safety
sections.content:
**AtomicInteger** is a thread-safe integer wrapper from the `java.util.concurrent.atomic` package that provides atomic operations without using locks. Unlike synchronized, which blocks threads waiting for a lock, AtomicInteger uses **compare-and-swap (CAS)**—a CPU-level hardware instruction that atomically checks if a value equals an expected value and, if so, updates it to a new value in a single operation.

Think of CAS like an optimistic update: read the current value, compute the new value, then attempt to swap it in, but only if no one else changed it in the meantime. If the swap fails (someone else modified it), retry immediately. This **lock-free** approach avoids the overhead of OS-level context switching and blocking that synchronized incurs. For simple operations like incrementing a counter, AtomicInteger is significantly faster under high contention because failed CAS attempts just spin and retry in user space rather than blocking and waking threads. It's a foundational tool in modern concurrent Java programming, used internally by many concurrent collections and executors.

sections.title: Blocking Lock vs Lock-Free CAS
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[synchronized] --> S1[Thread blocks
if the lock is taken] A[AtomicInteger] --> A1[Compare and swap] A1 --> A2{Swap succeeded?} A2 -- No --> A1 A2 -- Yes --> A3[Done, never blocked] ```

sections.content:
amber|synchronized|~Lock-based|blocks other threads|any critical section|heavier under contention
blue|AtomicInteger|~Lock-free CAS|compare-and-swap|single-variable ops|scales better
emerald|When Atomic|~One variable|counters, flags|incrementAndGet()|no blocking
violet|When synchronized|~Multi-step invariants|compound updates|several fields|atomic class not enough

sections.content:
| Aspect | AtomicInteger | synchronized int |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Lock-free CAS (hardware) | Mutex lock (OS-level) |
| Blocking | Never blocks threads | Blocks waiting threads |
| Performance | Faster under contention | Slower due to context switching |
| Use case | Single variable updates | Multi-variable compound operations |
| Memory overhead | One object wrapper | Intrinsic lock on any object |

sections.title: synchronized — Correct but Blocks Every Thread
AtomicInteger — Lock-Free Compare-and-Swap
When to Use AtomicInteger vs synchronized
sections.content:
Use **AtomicInteger** when you need a thread-safe counter, flag, or single integer variable that multiple threads update independently. It's perfect for request counters in a web service, rate limiters, metrics, or retry counts. The atomic package also offers **AtomicLong**, **AtomicBoolean**, and **AtomicReference** for other primitive and reference types.

Use **synchronized** when you need to coordinate multiple variables in a single atomic operation—like updating both a counter and a timestamp together, or checking a condition and then modifying state. AtomicInteger can't protect multi-step logic. For example, a check-then-act pattern like if count less than limit then increment requires synchronized or explicit locking to be atomic. In high-throughput APIs where thousands of threads increment a shared counter, AtomicInteger will outperform synchronized significantly. But if your critical section involves complex logic, I/O, or multiple fields, use synchronized or **ReentrantLock** for clarity and correctness.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using AtomicInteger for compound operations**: Freshers call get then set thinking it's atomic, but get followed by set is two operations—another thread can change the value between them. Use **compareAndSet** or **updateAndGet** for atomic compound operations.
- **Not understanding CAS retry loops**: The incrementAndGet method internally uses a loop with compareAndSet—if contention is extremely high, it can spin many times, though it's still faster than blocking.
- **Mixing AtomicInteger with synchronized**: If some code uses atomic operations and other code uses synchronized on a different lock to access the same logical state, you still have race conditions—pick one concurrency strategy and stick to it.
- **Assuming all atomic class methods are lock-free**: Some methods like lazySet have weaker guarantees—read the javadoc to understand memory visibility semantics.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Compare-and-swap (CAS)**: A CPU instruction that atomically compares a memory location to an expected value and updates it only if it matches, returning success or failure
- **Non-blocking**: AtomicInteger operations never put a thread into a BLOCKED state—if a CAS fails, the method just retries immediately in a tight loop
- **incrementAndGet**: Atomically increments and returns the new value using an internal CAS loop—equivalent to plus-plus but thread-safe
- **compareAndSet**: The fundamental operation—atomically updates the value if it equals the expected value, returns true if successful
- **Memory visibility**: All atomic operations have volatile semantics—changes are immediately visible to all threads without explicit synchronization
- **Performance scaling**: Under high contention, AtomicInteger scales better than synchronized because it avoids kernel locks and context switches
- **Not a silver bullet**: AtomicInteger works for single-variable updates; complex multi-step operations still need synchronized or explicit locks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: AtomicInteger is a thread-safe integer class from the java dot util dot concurrent dot atomic package. It's different from synchronized because it doesn't use locks. Instead, it uses compare-and-swap, which is a special CPU instruction. Here's how CAS works. The thread reads the current value, computes the new value—like adding one—then tries to swap the new value in. But the swap only succeeds if the value hasn't changed since we read it. If another thread changed it, the CAS fails, and we retry. It's like an optimistic lock. This is way faster than synchronized because threads don't block. With synchronized, if one thread holds the lock, other threads go into a blocked state. The OS has to context-switch them out and wake them up later. That's expensive. With AtomicInteger, threads never block. If a CAS fails, they just retry immediately in a tight loop. No OS involvement. So under high contention, AtomicInteger scales much better. You'd use it for simple counters—like counting web requests or tracking metrics. Just call incrementAndGet and you're done. You'd use synchronized when you need to update multiple variables together atomically, or when you have complex logic. AtomicInteger can't protect multi-step operations. One mistake freshers make is calling get then set thinking it's atomic. It's not—another thread can change the value between get and set. You have to use compareAndSet or incrementAndGet, which are truly atomic. Another thing is AtomicInteger is part of the java dot util dot concurrent package, which has tons of useful classes like AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, ConcurrentHashMap. Learning this package is key for production Java.

questions.question: What is deadlock in Java and how can it occur?
questions.title: Deadlock in Java
questions.direct_answer: Deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock that another thread holds. It occurs in a circular dependency: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1—neither can proceed, and the application freezes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of deadlock as the main pitfall of synchronized programming and multi-threaded systems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing deadlock vaguely as threads waiting for each other without showing the concrete lock acquisition order that causes it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the classic two-lock example with bank account transfers and explain the lock ordering prevention technique—always acquire locks in a consistent global order.

sections.title: Understanding Deadlock: The Circular Wait Problem
sections.content:
**Deadlock** is a catastrophic state where two or more threads are stuck forever, each waiting for a resource (usually a lock) held by another thread in the group. No thread can proceed, and the application hangs indefinitely. It's the multi-threading equivalent of two cars blocking each other at a narrow intersection, neither able to reverse. Deadlock requires four conditions to occur simultaneously: **mutual exclusion** (locks can be held by only one thread), **hold and wait** (a thread holding one lock requests another), **no preemption** (you can't forcibly take a lock from a thread), and **circular wait** (Thread A waits for Thread B's lock while B waits for A's).

In Java, the circular wait is the key. Imagine transferring money between bank accounts: Thread 1 locks Account A, then tries to lock Account B. Simultaneously, Thread 2 locks Account B, then tries to lock Account A. Thread 1 waits for B (held by Thread 2), Thread 2 waits for A (held by Thread 1). Neither releases what they hold. The JVM can't detect or break this automatically—your application freezes until you restart it. **Lock ordering** is the classic prevention strategy: always acquire locks in a consistent global order (e.g., by account ID).

sections.title: The Circular Wait That Forms a Deadlock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR T1[Thread 1
holds Lock A] -->|waits for| LB[Lock B] T2[Thread 2
holds Lock B] -->|waits for| LA[Lock A] LB --> T2 LA --> T1 ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Deadlock|~Permanent block|each waits on the other|circular wait|no progress ever
blue|Cause|~Nested locks|lock A then B|other locks B then A|opposite order
emerald|Prevention|~Break the cycle|global lock ordering|tryLock with timeout|fewer locks
violet|Detection|~Find it|thread dump|deadlock section|jstack / monitoring

sections.title: Wrong: lock order depends on the arguments
Right: always lock the lower id first
Where Deadlocks Occur in Production
sections.content:
Deadlocks happen when your code acquires multiple locks in different orders across different execution paths. The classic scenario is resource ordering problems: transferring between accounts, moving items between inventories, or updating related database records where different threads lock resources in opposite sequences. In Spring applications with nested synchronized methods, if Service A calls Service B while holding a lock, and Service B calls back to Service A, you risk deadlock. Database transactions can deadlock at the JDBC level if two transactions update rows in different orders. Even seemingly safe code like synchronized collections can deadlock if you synchronize on multiple collections in a chain of operations. The key is identifying where you hold one lock while requesting another.

Use **lock ordering** (always acquire in ID order), **lock timeout** with tryLock from **ReentrantLock**, or redesign to eliminate the need for multiple locks by using immutable data structures or atomic compound operations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested synchronized blocks on different objects**: Freshers write code that locks object A, then inside that block locks object B, without realizing another method locks B then A—this creates the circular wait condition.
- **Ignoring lock acquisition order**: Not establishing a consistent global order for acquiring locks across all code paths that touch the same resources.
- **Thinking deadlock only happens with explicit locks**: Deadlock can occur with any blocking resource—database row locks, file locks, even joining threads in circular dependency patterns.
- **No timeout mechanism**: Using plain synchronized instead of ReentrantLock with tryLock means threads wait forever—there's no way to detect or recover from deadlock automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Circular dependency**: Deadlock requires a cycle—Thread A waits for B, B waits for C, C waits for A (or any closed loop of dependencies)
- **Two locks minimum**: You need at least two locks for deadlock; single-lock systems can't deadlock (though they can have other issues like starvation)
- **Lock ordering prevention**: Always acquire locks in a consistent order across all threads—sort by object ID, memory address, or any total ordering
- **tryLock with timeout**: ReentrantLock offers tryLock that returns false if the lock isn't available within a timeout, letting you back off and retry
- **Thread dumps**: When an app freezes, taking a thread dump (jstack or kill -3) shows threads in BLOCKED state waiting for monitors, revealing deadlock cycles
- **Immutable data**: Using immutable objects eliminates the need for locking—if data never changes, threads can read freely without coordination
- **Database deadlocks**: JDBC and JPA can cause deadlocks at the database level if transactions update rows in different orders—this is separate from Java thread deadlocks but similar in concept

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Deadlock happens when two or more threads are stuck waiting for each other forever. Neither can move forward. The classic example is two threads each holding one lock and trying to get the other's lock. Thread A locks Account X and tries to lock Account Y. At the same time, Thread B locks Account Y and tries to lock Account X. Thread A can't proceed until it gets Y, but Thread B holds Y and won't release it until it gets X. Thread B can't proceed until it gets X, but Thread A holds X. They're stuck in a circle. Your application just freezes. The JVM doesn't detect or break deadlocks automatically—you have to prevent them in your code. The standard way to prevent deadlock is consistent lock ordering. Always acquire locks in the same order everywhere in your code. For bank accounts, you might sort by account ID and always lock the lower ID first, then the higher ID. That way, no matter which direction you're transferring money, you acquire locks in the same sequence. No circular wait, no deadlock. Another approach is using ReentrantLock with tryLock. You can specify a timeout—if you don't get the lock in say one second, tryLock returns false. Then you release any locks you're holding, wait a bit, and retry. That breaks the circular wait. Freshers often nest synchronized blocks without thinking about order. They lock object A then B in one method, and B then A in another method. That's a deadlock waiting to happen. Always be aware of what locks you hold and what order you acquire them in.

beats.text: Deadlock happens when two threads each hold a lock the other needs. Thread A holds the first lock and waits for the second. Thread B holds the second and waits for the first. Neither one lets go. They're stuck forever.

Deadlock grows out of nested locking. Each `synchronized` block looks fine on its own. The trouble starts when two threads grab the same two locks in opposite orders. That forms a cycle that can't resolve.

items: Mutual exclusion: only one thread can hold a lock.
Hold and wait: a thread keeps one lock while it asks for another.
No preemption: nobody can force a lock away from a thread.

beats.text: Picture a bank transfer between two accounts. Thread 1 locks account A, then account B. Thread 2 locks account B, then account A. Here's the sharp edge. questions.question: What is the visibility problem in multithreading and how does synchronization address it?
questions.title: Visibility Problem in Java Multithreading
questions.direct_answer: The visibility problem occurs when one thread's write to a shared variable isn't visible to other threads due to CPU caching—each core may cache values locally and not immediately write changes to main memory. When a thread exits a synchronized block, the JVM flushes its cache to main memory, and when another thread enters a synchronized block, it invalidates its cache and reads fresh values, guaranteeing visibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java Memory Model basics—synchronized does more than just prevent simultaneous execution, it also ensures memory consistency.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking synchronized only prevents race conditions through atomicity, without realizing it also solves the visibility problem through memory barriers.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java Memory Model (JMM) and the happens-before relationship—synchronized creates ordering guarantees that ensure writes before releasing a lock are visible to reads after acquiring the same lock.

sections.title: The Visibility Problem and Memory Consistency
sections.content:
The **visibility problem** is a subtle multi-threading issue where one thread modifies a shared variable, but other threads continue seeing the old value indefinitely. This happens because modern CPUs don't write every change directly to main memory. Each core has its own **cache hierarchy** (L1, L2, sometimes L3) for performance. When a thread writes to a variable, it might update only its local cache, not main memory. Other threads reading that variable might also be using their cached copy, never seeing the update. From the programmer's perspective, it looks like writes are lost or delayed. The **Java Memory Model (JMM)** defines when writes by one thread become visible to other threads.

Without explicit synchronization, the JMM allows aggressive optimizations—caching, reordering instructions, even eliminating dead writes. The **synchronized** keyword creates **memory barriers** (also called fences): when a thread exits a synchronized block, all its writes are flushed to main memory, and when another thread enters a synchronized block on the same lock, it invalidates its cache and reads fresh values. This **happens-before** relationship ensures memory consistency. The **volatile** keyword provides a lighter-weight solution for single variables, guaranteeing visibility without locking.

sections.title: Why a Stale Cache Hides a Write
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB W[Thread A writes value] --> C1[Lives in core 1 cache] C1 --> M[Main memory
not updated yet] R[Thread B reads value] --> C2[Reads core 2 cache] C2 --> St[Sees a stale value] M --> Sync[synchronized or volatile
flushes and refreshes] Sync --> F[Fresh value is seen] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Visibility Problem|~Stale reads|thread caches a value|write not seen|loop never ends
blue|Cause|~CPU caches and JIT|per-core caches|reordering|no flush
emerald|volatile Fix|~Visibility only|read/write main memory|happens-before|no atomicity
violet|synchronized Fix|~Visibility plus mutex|flush on release|acquire sees writes|covers compound ops

sections.title: Wrong: a non-volatile flag can be cached forever
Right: synchronized publishes the writes
Ensuring Visibility in Practice
sections.content:
Use **synchronized** to guarantee visibility when protecting compound operations or multiple related variables. Every exit from a synchronized block flushes writes to main memory, and every entry invalidates cached reads. For single variable flags like stop signals or initialization checks, use **volatile** instead—it's lighter weight than synchronized because it doesn't involve locking. Volatile ensures every write is immediately visible to all threads and reads always fetch the latest value.

Use **AtomicInteger** and related classes from java.util.concurrent.atomic for thread-safe single-variable updates—they have built-in volatile semantics plus atomic operations. Be aware that final fields initialized in a constructor are safely published—once the constructor completes, all threads see the final values without extra synchronization. In Spring beans, immutable configuration objects (@ConfigurationProperties) leverage this. Never rely on plain reads and writes to shared non-volatile variables—the JVM is allowed to reorder or cache them in ways that violate your expectations of sequential execution.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing writes but not reads**: Freshers protect the write with synchronized but leave reads unsynchronized—reads will still see stale cached values because they don't acquire the lock that triggers cache invalidation.
- **Assuming volatile solves race conditions**: Volatile guarantees visibility but not atomicity—count plus plus on a volatile int still has a race condition because it's three operations (read, increment, write).
- **Ignoring happens-before**: Not realizing that synchronized creates ordering guarantees between threads—writes before releasing a lock are visible to subsequent acquisitions of the same lock.
- **Over-relying on eventual consistency**: Thinking writes will eventually become visible without synchronization—the JMM provides no time bound, so threads might spin forever seeing stale values.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CPU caching**: Each core caches memory in local L1/L2 caches for speed—writes may stay in cache without reaching main memory immediately
- **Java Memory Model (JMM)**: The specification defining when writes by one thread become visible to reads by another thread
- **Memory barrier**: A fence operation that flushes caches and enforces ordering—synchronized creates barriers at entry and exit of blocks
- **Happens-before relationship**: A JMM guarantee that if action A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B—synchronized establishes happens-before
- **Volatile keyword**: A lighter-weight alternative to synchronized that guarantees visibility for a single variable without locking
- **Double-checked locking**: A broken pattern without volatile—checking a field outside synchronized then inside can see partially constructed objects due to reordering
- **Safe publication**: Final fields and properly synchronized initialization ensure objects are safely published to other threads without seeing partially constructed state

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The visibility problem is when one thread updates a variable but other threads don't see the change. It happens because of CPU caching. Modern processors don't write every change directly to main memory. Each CPU core has its own cache—L1, L2 cache layers. When Thread A writes to a variable, it might just update its local cache. Thread B, running on a different core, has its own cached copy of that variable. It keeps reading the old value from its cache. From the code's perspective, it looks like the write disappeared. Without synchronization, the JVM and CPU are allowed to do this for performance. The Java Memory Model defines the rules. It says you need explicit synchronization to guarantee visibility. That's what synchronized does. When a thread exits a synchronized block, it flushes all its writes to main memory. When another thread enters a synchronized block on the same lock, it invalidates its cache and reads fresh values from main memory. This is called a happens-before relationship. The synchronized keyword creates memory barriers that enforce ordering and visibility. It's not just about preventing race conditions through mutual exclusion. It also solves the caching problem. The volatile keyword is another solution. If you mark a variable as volatile, every write goes directly to main memory, and every read comes from main memory. No caching. It's lighter weight than synchronized because there's no lock, but it only works for single variables. A common mistake freshers make is thinking synchronized only prevents interleaving. They protect writes with synchronized but leave reads plain. Those reads will still see stale cached values. You have to synchronize both reads and writes on the same lock to get the happens-before guarantee.

beats.text: Picture a thread looping while a `running` flag stays true. Another thread sets that flag to false. Here's the non-obvious part. The looping thread can cache the old true value and spin forever. It never sees the change. Marking the flag `volatile`, or guarding it with `synchronized`, forces a fresh read.

Without `volatile` or `synchronized`, one thread's flag change might never reach another.
